title: The class of Banach lattices is not primary
author: Antonio Acuaviva
abstract: Building on a recent construction of Plebanek and Salguero-Alarcón, which solved the Complemented Subspace Problem for \(C(K)\)-spaces, and the subsequent work of De Hevia, Martínez-Cervantes, Salguero-Alarcón, and Tradacete solving the Complemented Subspace Problem for Banach lattices, we show that the class of Banach lattices is not primary. Specifically, we exhibit a compact Hausdorff space \(L\) such that \(C(L)\simeq X\oplus\tilde{X}\) and neither \(X\) nor \(\tilde{X}\) is isomorphic to a Banach lattice. In particular, it also follows that the class of \(C(K)\)-spaces is not primary.

1.

Introduction and main results

−

In a remarkable construction, Plebanek and Salguero-Alarcón constructed compact Hausdorff spaces \(K\) and \(L\) such that \(C(L)\simeq C(K)\oplus\mathrm{PS}_{2}\) and the Banach space \(\mathrm{PS}_{2}\) fails to be isomorphic to a \(C(K)\)-space, giving a negative solution to the longstanding Complemented Subspace Problem for \(C(K)\)-spaces. Shortly after, De Hevia, Martínez-Cervantes, Salguero-Alarcón, and Tradacete showed that the space \(\mathrm{PS}_{2}\) is not even isomorphic to a Banach lattice, thus providing a negative solution to the Complemented Subspace Problem for Banach lattices.

Building on these results, we show that the class of Banach lattices is not primary. More precisely, we obtain the following.

There exist a compact Hausdorff space \(L\) and Banach spaces \(X\) and \(\tilde{X}\) such that

\(C(L)\simeq X\oplus\tilde{X},\)

and neither \(X\) nor \(\tilde{X}\) is isomorphic to a Banach lattice.

In particular, this answers a question of De Hevia and Tradacete , which originally motivated our interest in this problem. Observe that this also implies that the class of \(C(K)\)-spaces is not primary.

Finally, in passing, we note that, with natural modifications, the arguments in show that the same conclusion holds for complex Banach lattices.

2.

Organization and sketch of the proof of Theorem 1.1

−

Our construction builds on the construction of Plebanek and Salguero-Alarcón , together with the subsequent work of De Hevia, Martínez-Cervantes, Salguero-Alarcón, and Tradacete .

Section 3 introduces basic terminology and recalls concepts necessary for the construction. This section also builds the framework in which the construction will be performed. Section 4 reformulates some results of Plebanek and Salguero-Alarcón in our setting. The reader familiar with their work can safely skim this section and refer back to it as and when needed. Since the proofs of these modified results are essentially the same as in the work of Plebanek and Salguero-Alarcón, we either omit them or provide only outlines of the necessary changes, as appropriate.

Section 5 contains the construction of the counterexample. The idea is as follows. Plebanek and Salguero-Alarcón constructed compact Hausdorff spaces \(K\) and \(L\) such that

\(C(L)=C(K)\oplus\mathrm{PS}_{2}\)

and \(\mathrm{PS}_{2}\) fails to be a isomorphic to a \(C(K)\)-space.

Their approach relies on a transfinite construction that rules out the existence of a weak∗-compact subset of \(B_{\mathrm{PS}_{2}^{*}}\) which is both norming and free.

In our setting, we perform two such constructions simultaneously, producing four compact Hausdorff spaces \(K\), \(\tilde{K}\), \(L\), and \(\tilde{L}\) such that

\(C(L)=C(K)\oplus Y,\quad C(\tilde{L})=C(\tilde{K})\oplus\tilde{Y}.\)

This simultaneous approach allows us to intertwine the structure of \(K\) with \(\tilde{Y}\) and that of \(\tilde{K}\) with \(Y\) so that neither

\(X:=C(\tilde{K})\oplus Y\quad\text{nor}\quad\tilde{X}:=C(K)\oplus\tilde{Y}\) (1)

is isomorphic to a Banach lattice, but clearly

\(X\oplus\tilde{X}=(C(\tilde{K})\oplus Y)\oplus(C(K)\oplus\tilde{Y})=C(L)\oplus C(\tilde{L})=C(L\sqcup\tilde{L}),\)

where \(L\sqcup\tilde{L}\) denotes the topological sum of \(L\) and \(\tilde{L}\).

The proof that the Banach spaces \(X\) and \(\tilde{X}\) defined by (1) are not isomorphic to Banach lattices is now essentially the same as the one in . We include the details in Section 6 for the reader’s convenience.

We stress that the underlying idea remains the same as in Plebanek and Salguero-Alarcón’s work: there are sufficiently many possible choices in their construction (in fact, continuum many), which enables us to select ones that prevent \(X\) and \(\tilde{X}\) from being isomorphic to Banach lattices.

3.

Preliminaries

−
3.1.

Johnson-Lindenstrauss spaces, Boolean algebras, and Alexandrov-Urysohn compacta.

−

We denote by \(\omega=\{0,1,2\dots,\}\) the set of non-negative integers and let \(\operatorname{fin}(\omega)\) be the family of all finite subsets of \(\omega\). Given \(\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\omega)\), we let \([\mathcal{F}]\) denote the smallest Boolean subalgebra of \(\mathcal{P}(\omega)\) containing \(\mathcal{F}\).

A family \(\mathcal{B}\) of infinite subsets of \(\omega\) (or of any other countably infinite set) is called almost disjoint if for every distinct pair \(A,B\in\mathcal{B}\) the intersection \(A\cap B\) is finite. Given an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{B}\), the Johnson-Lindenstrauss space \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B})\) is the closed linear span inside of \(\ell_{\infty}\) of the set of characteristic functions

\(\{\mathds{1}_{n}:n\in\omega\}\cup\{\mathds{1}_{B}:B\in\mathcal{B}\}\cup\{\mathds{1}_{\omega}\},\)

where \(\mathds{1}_{n}\) stands for \(\mathds{1}_{\{n\}}\). Alternatively, let \(\mathfrak{B}=[\mathcal{B\cup\operatorname{fin}(\omega)}]\), then \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B})\) is the closed linear span of simple \(\mathfrak{B}\)-measurable functions, that is, functions of the form \(f=\sum_{i\leq n}r_{i}\mathds{1}_{B_{i}}\), where \(n\in\omega\), \(r_{i}\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(B_{i}\in\mathfrak{B}\). It is known that \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B})\) is isometrically isomorphic to a \(C(K)\)-space. The underlying compact Hausdorff space \(\operatorname*{ult}(\mathfrak{B})\) is the Stone space of the Boolean algebra \(\mathfrak{B}\). Equivalently, this space can be explicitly realized as follows. Define \(K_{\mathcal{B}}=\omega\cup\{p_{B}:B\in\mathcal{B\}}\cup\{\infty\}\), and specify a topology on \(K_{\mathcal{B}}\) by

  • •

    points in \(\omega\) are isolated,

  • •

    for every \(B\in\mathcal{B}\), a neighbourhoods basis \(p_{B}\) is given by the sets \(p_{B}\cup(B\setminus F)\) where \(F\in\operatorname{fin}(\omega)\),

  • •

    \(K_{\mathcal{B}}\) is the one-point compactification of the locally compact Hausdorff space \(\omega\cup\{p_{B}:B\in\mathcal{B\}}\), endowed with the above topology.

It is easy to see that this space is a separable, scattered, compact Hausdorff space with empty third Cantor-Bendixson derivative. Observe that the dual of \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B})\) is isometrically isomorphic to the space \(M(\mathfrak{B})\) of real-valued finitely additive measures on \(\mathfrak{B}\) of finite variation.

3.2.

The space \(M(\mathfrak{B})\).

−

The measures in \(M(\mathfrak{B})\) have a nice description. Since \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B})\) is isometrically isomorphic to \(C(K_{\mathcal{B}})\), where \(K_{\mathcal{B}}\) is scattered, the Riesz Representation Theorem and Rudin’s theorem imply that

\(M(\mathfrak{B})=\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B})^{*}=C(K_{\mathcal{B}})^{*}=\ell_{1}(K_{\mathcal{B}});\)

that is, every measure \(\nu\in M(\mathfrak{B})\) can be expressed as

\(\nu=\sum_{s\in K_{\mathcal{B}}}c_{s}\delta_{s}\)

for some scalars \(c_{s}\in\mathbb{R}\), so that

\(\left\lVert\nu\right\rVert_{1}=\sum_{s\in K_{\mathcal{B}}}|c_{s}|.\)

In particular, we can decompose \(\nu\) as

\(\nu=\mu+\overline{\nu},\hskip 5.0pt\text{ where }\hskip 5.0pt\mu=\sum_{s\in\omega}c_{s}\delta_{s}\hskip 5.0pt\text{ and }\hskip 5.0pt\overline{\nu}=\sum_{s\in K_{\mathcal{B}}\setminus\omega}c_{s}\delta_{s}.\)

We will call \(\mu\) the \(\ell_{1}(\omega)\)-part of \(\nu\).

The coordinate at infinity

The printed coordinate description below omits the atom at infinity. Evaluation there vanishes on singleton and family indicators but is one on the constant function. The Lean representation retains this coordinate, and both copies are carried through the later construction. The explanatory notes for Theorem 1.1 describe this difference.

For our purposes, we will usually have an enumeration of the almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{B}=\{B_{\xi}:\xi<\mathfrak{c\}}\), in that case, we can further identify

\(M(\mathfrak{B})=\ell_{1}(\omega)\oplus\ell_{1}(\mathfrak{c})\)

in a canonical way. It is worthwhile to pause briefly to expand on this representation of \(M(\mathfrak{B})\), as this will play an important role later.

Observe that given an element \(x\in\ell_{1}(\omega)\), we can naturally consider it as a measure \(\mu\in M(\mathcal{P}(\omega))\) by

\(\mu(B)=\sum_{s\in B}x(s),\hskip 5.0ptB\subseteq\omega.\)

Furthermore, considering the restriction of \(\mu\) to the Boolean subalgebra \(\mathfrak{B}\) of \(\mathcal{P}(\omega)\), we can consider \(\mu\in M(\mathfrak{B})\).

Note that this provides a key insight: the \(\ell_{1}(\omega)\)-part has, in a sense, a universal character, as it extends uniquely as a measure to any Boolean subalgebra of \(\mathcal{P}(\omega)\).

Now, given a measure \(\nu\in M(\mathfrak{B})\), we can decompose \(\nu=\mu+\overline{\nu}\), where \(\mu\in M(\mathfrak{B})\) arises from an element \(x\) of \(\ell_{1}(\omega)\) and \(\overline{\nu}\) vanishes on finite sets. Moreover, \(|\overline{\nu}|(B)\neq 0\) for at most countably many \(B\in\mathcal{B}\), so we may identify \(\overline{\nu}\) with an element \(y\in\ell_{1}(\mathfrak{c})\) by setting \(y(\alpha)=\overline{\nu}(B_{\alpha})\) for \(\alpha<\mathfrak{c}\). Conversely, given \(y\in\ell_{1}(\mathfrak{c})\), we may associate to it a measure \(\overline{\nu}\in M(\mathfrak{B})\) in this way. Thus, we may represent any \(\nu\in M(\mathfrak{B})\) by a pair \((x,y)\in\ell_{1}(\omega)\oplus\ell_{1}(\mathfrak{c})\), where \(x\) corresponds to \(\mu\) and \(y\) to \(\overline{\nu}\). Conversely, every \((x,y)\in\ell_{1}(\omega)\oplus\ell_{1}(\mathfrak{c})\) determines a measure \(\nu=\mu+\overline{\nu}\in M(\mathfrak{B})\).

We now record a crucial observation. For any ordinal \(\xi<\mathfrak{c}\) consider the subalgebra \(\mathfrak{B}(\xi)\) of \(\mathfrak{B}\) given by

\(\mathfrak{B}(\xi)=[\{B_{\alpha}:\alpha<\xi\}\cup\operatorname{fin}(\omega)]\subseteq\mathfrak{B},\)

and let \(\nu\in M(\mathfrak{B}(\xi))\). Then \(\nu\) naturally extends to an element of \(M(\mathfrak{B})\). As above, we decompose \(\nu=\mu+\overline{\nu}\), where \(\mu\) is the \(\ell_{1}(\omega)\)-part of \(\nu\). Observe that \(\mu\) naturally defines a measure in \(M(\mathfrak{B})\), while \(\overline{\nu}\) can be extended to \(M(\mathfrak{B})\) by declaring \(\overline{\nu}(B_{\alpha})=0\) for every \(\xi\leq\alpha<\mathfrak{c}\).

Conversely, suppose \(\nu\in M(\mathfrak{B})\) and decompose \(\nu=\mu+\overline{\nu}\), where \(\mu\) is the \(\ell_{1}(\omega)\)-part of \(\nu\). Since \(|\overline{\nu}|(B)\neq 0\) for only countably many \(B\in\mathfrak{B}\), there exists \(\xi<\mathfrak{c}\) such that \(|\overline{\nu}|(B_{\alpha})=0\) for all \(\alpha\geq\xi\). In particular, we can identify \(\nu\) with a measure in \(M(\mathfrak{B}(\xi))\), corresponding to its restriction to \(\mathfrak{B}(\xi)\). Observe that the natural extension of the latter recovers \(\nu\).

3.3.

Complemented subspaces.

−

As in the original work of Plebanek and Salguero-Alarcón, it will be convenient to work with \(\omega\times 2\) instead of \(\omega\). Every subset \(C\) of the form \(C=C_{0}\times 2\) for some \(C_{0}\subseteq\omega\) is called a cylinder. For \(n\in\omega\) we denote by \(c_{n}\) the cylinder \(\{(n,0),(n,1)\}\). We say that a set \(B\subseteq C\) splits the cylinder \(C\) if \(|B\cap c_{n}|=1\) whenever \(c_{n}\subseteq C\). Observe that in this case \(C\setminus B\) also splits \(C\), and we say that \(B\) and \(C\setminus B\) is a splitting of \(C\).

Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}=\{A_{\xi}:\xi<\mathfrak{c\}}\) is an almost disjoint family of cylinders in \(\omega\times 2\), together with a splitting \(B^{i}_{\xi}\), \(i=0,1\) of each cylinder \(A_{\xi}\). Observe that then \(\mathcal{B}=\{B^{0}_{\xi},B^{1}_{\xi}:\xi<\mathfrak{c}\}\) is also an almost disjoint family. In this situation, we will say that the almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{B}\) splits \(\mathcal{A}\).

In this setting, we can find a \(1\)-complemented isometric copy of \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{A})\) inside \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B})\), see . With a slight abuse of notation, we will continue to denote this copy by \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{A})\). More precisely, this copy is the closed linear subspace of \(\ell_{\infty}(\omega\times 2)\) spanned by

\(\{\mathds{1}_{c_{n}}:n\in\omega\}\cup\{\mathds{1}_{A}:A\in\mathcal{A}\}\cup\{\mathds{1}_{\omega\times 2}\}.\)

Equivalently, in the definition of \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{A})\), we restrict to finite cylinders rather than all finite subsets of \(\omega\times 2\).

It is worthwhile to briefly recall how \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{A})\) sits inside \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B})\). Concretely, \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{A})\) consists of those functions in \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B})\) which are constant on cylinders. The map \(P:\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B})\to\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B})\) defined by

\(Pf(n,0)=Pf(n,1)=\tfrac{1}{2}\big(f(n,0)+f(n,1)\big)\)

is a norm-one projection. We denote \(Y=\ker P\), which can be explicitly described as

\(Y=\{f\in\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B}):f(n,0)=-f(n,1)\text{ for all }n\in\omega\}.\)

Thus, we obtain the decomposition

\(C(K_{\mathcal{B}})=\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B})=\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{A})\oplus Y,\) (2)

which is precisely the content of . Observe that by the discussion on Subsections 3.1 and 3.2, we can naturally identify

\(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B})^{*}=M(\mathfrak{B})=C(K_{\mathcal{B}})^{*}=\ell_{1}(\omega\times 2)\oplus\ell_{1}(\mathcal{B})=\ell_{1}(\omega\times 2)\oplus\ell_{1}(\mathfrak{c}\times 2),\)

where \(\mathfrak{B}=[\mathcal{B}\cup\operatorname{fin}(\omega\times 2)]\).

3.4.

Two spaces.

−

As we mentioned before, we will need to carry out two simultaneous constructions and thus, to avoid confusion, it is convenient to use the distinctive notation \(\tilde{\omega}\times 2\) for the second copy of \(\omega\times 2\) in which the second construction will be carried out.

We emphasize that the absence of a tilde indicates we are working in \(\omega\times 2\), whereas a tilde denotes objects in \(\tilde{\omega}\times 2\). For instance, a cylinder \(C\) is understood to satisfy \(C\subseteq\omega\times 2\), while a cylinder \(\tilde{C}\) satisfies \(\tilde{C}\subseteq\tilde{\omega}\times 2\). It will also be convenient to sometimes use this when we are working with index sets. For example, we may write \((\tilde{c}_{\tilde{n}})_{\tilde{n}\in\tilde{\omega}}\). When there is no ambiguity, we may simply omit the tilde in the index. In all cases, the intended meaning should be clear from the context.

Therefore, in our construction, we will build two almost disjoint families \(\mathcal{B}=\{B^{0}_{\xi},B^{1}_{\xi}:\xi<\mathfrak{c}\}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\omega\times 2)\) and \(\tilde{\mathcal{B}}=\{\tilde{B}^{0}_{\xi},\tilde{B}^{1}_{\xi}:\xi<\mathfrak{c}\}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\omega}\times 2)\) splitting almost disjoint families of cylinders \(\mathcal{A}=\{A_{\xi}:\xi<\mathfrak{c}\}\) and \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}=\{\tilde{A}_{\xi}:\xi<\mathfrak{c}\}\). From the discussion above (2), it follows that

\(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B})=\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{A})\oplus Y\hskip 5.0pt\text{ and }\hskip 5.0pt\operatorname{JL}(\tilde{\mathcal{B}})=\operatorname{JL}(\tilde{\mathcal{A}})\oplus\tilde{Y},\)

so that

\(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B})\oplus\operatorname{JL}(\tilde{\mathcal{B}})=(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{A})\oplus Y)\oplus(\operatorname{JL}(\tilde{\mathcal{A}})\oplus\tilde{Y})=X\oplus\tilde{X},\)

where \(X:=\operatorname{JL}(\tilde{A})\oplus Y\) and \(\tilde{X}:=\operatorname{JL}(A)\oplus\tilde{Y}\). Observe that this is precisely the setting in (1), bearing in mind that \(\operatorname{JL}(\cdot)\) are isometric to \(C(K)\)-spaces.

For brevity, we write

\(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B},\tilde{\mathcal{B}})=\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B})\oplus\operatorname{JL}(\tilde{\mathcal{B}})\hskip 5.0pt\text{ and }\hskip 5.0ptM(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})=\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B},\tilde{\mathcal{B}})^{*}=M(\mathfrak{B})\oplus M(\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}).\)

We denote by \(Q\) and \(\tilde{Q}\) the norm-one projections of \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B},\tilde{\mathcal{B}})\) onto \(X\) and \(\tilde{X}\), respectively.

Furthermore, we denote by \(M_{1}(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\) the unit ball of \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B},\tilde{\mathcal{B}})^{*}\), equipped with the weak∗ topology. We can naturally view \(M(\mathfrak{B})\) and \(M(\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\) as subsets of \(M(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\). In this spirit, any measure \(\nu\in M(\mathfrak{B})\) can be regarded as an element of \(M(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\), and similarly for \(\tilde{\nu}\in M(\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\). Naturally, any measure \(\lambda\in M(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\) can be decomposed as \(\lambda=\nu+\tilde{\nu}\) where \(\nu\in M(\mathfrak{B})\) and \(\tilde{\nu}\in M(\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\).

3.5.

Norming sets and Banach lattices.

−

Our overall aim is to prove that, for a suitable choice of the families \(\mathcal{A},\tilde{\mathcal{A}},\mathcal{B}\) and \(\tilde{\mathcal{B}}\), the resulting spaces \(X\) and \(\tilde{X}\) are not isomorphic to Banach lattices. Therefore, we recall the conditions from that ensure that this to occurs. We denote by \(B_{X}\) the unit ball of a Banach space \(X\).

Let \(X\) be a Banach space and \(0<c\leq 1\). We say that a sequence \((e_{n}^{*})_{n\in\omega}\subseteq B_{X^{*}}\) is \(c\)-norming if

\(c\left\lVert x\right\rVert\leq\sup_{n\in\omega}|\langle e^{*}_{n},x\rangle|\)

for every \(x\in X\). If the constant \(c\) is not relevant, we simply say that the sequence \((e_{n}^{*})_{n\in\omega}\subseteq B_{X^{*}}\) is norming.

We say that a Banach space \(X\) has the Desired Property of De Hevia, Martínez-Cervantes, Salguero-Alarcón, and Tradacete, abbreviated (DP), if for every norming sequence \((e_{n}^{*})_{n\in\omega}\) in \(B_{X^{*}}\) there exists an element \(f\in X\) such that no element \(g\in X\) satisfies

\(\langle e_{n}^{*},g\rangle=|\langle e_{n}^{*},f\rangle|\quad\text{for every }n\in\omega.\) (DP)

The motivation behind the previous definition is that, under certain conditions, satisfying (DP) implies that the space is not isomorphic to a Banach lattice. In particular, we have the following, see .

Let \(X\) be a Banach space with a countable norming set. Suppose that \(X^{*}\) is isomorphic to \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\) for some index set \(\Gamma\). Then, the following statements are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    \(X\) is isomorphic to a Banach lattice.

  2. (b)

    \(X\) is isomorphic to a sublattice of \(\ell_{\infty}\).

  3. (c)

    \(X\) does not have the (DP). That is, there exists a norming sequence \((e_{n}^{*})_{n\in\omega}\) in \(B_{X^{*}}\) such that for every \(f\in X\) there is an element \(g\in X\) such that

    \(\langle e_{n}^{*},g\rangle=|\langle e_{n}^{*},f\rangle|,\quad\text{for every }n\in\omega.\)

We note that, for any almost disjoint families \(\mathcal{A},\tilde{\mathcal{A}},\mathcal{B}\) and \(\tilde{\mathcal{B}}\), the spaces \(X\) and \(\tilde{X}\), defined in Subsection 3.4, satisfy the conditions of Proposition 3.4 (see Section 6 for details). Therefore, to prove they are not isomorphic to Banach lattices, it is enough to show that they satisfy (DP).

3.6.

The spaces \(M(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\), \(X^{*}\) and \(\tilde{X}^{*}\).

−

Let \(\mathcal{A},\tilde{\mathcal{A}},\mathcal{B}\) and \(\tilde{\mathcal{B}}\) be almost disjoint families and \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{B})=X\oplus\tilde{X}\) as in the setting of Subsection 3.4. To ensure that \(X\) and \(\tilde{X}\) are not isomorphic to Banach lattices, it will be necessary to have control over the elements in the duals \(X^{*}\) and \(\tilde{X}^{*}\).

We start with the following observation, which is the analogue of . Recall that \(Q\) and \(\tilde{Q}\) denote the projections onto \(X\) and \(\tilde{X}\), respectively.

Let \(x^{*}\in X^{*}\). Then \(x^{*}Q\in\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B},\tilde{\mathcal{B}})^{*}=M(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\), so that every functional on \(X\) can be seen as an element on \(M(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\) vanishing on all cylinders from \(\mathfrak{B}\). In other words, we have an embedding

\(X^{*}\to M(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}),\quad x^{*}\mapsto x^{*}Q.\)

Analogous considerations apply to \(\tilde{x}^{*}\in\tilde{X}^{*}\).

Thus, from now on, when we consider an element in the dual of \(X\) or \(\tilde{X}\), we will always think of it as the measure in \(M(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\) representing it.

We will reserve the symbols \(\lambda\) and \(\gamma\) for elements in \(M_{1}(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\). Observe that we have a decomposition \(\lambda=\nu+\tilde{\nu}\) where \(\nu\in M_{1}(\mathfrak{B})\) and \(\tilde{\nu}\in M_{1}(\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\) (with their natural interpretations). From the discussion in Subsection 3.2, we can further express \(\nu=\mu+\overline{\nu}\) where \(\mu\in\ell_{1}(\omega\times 2)\), \(\overline{\nu}\) vanishes on finite sets and \(|\overline{\nu}|(B)\not=0\) for at most countably many \(B\in\mathcal{B}\). Identical considerations apply for \(\tilde{\nu}\). Using these decompositions we can write \(\lambda=\nu+\tilde{\nu}=(\mu+\overline{\nu})+(\tilde{\mu}+\tilde{\overline{\nu}})\). Therefore, a measure \(\lambda\in M_{1}(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\) can be seem as a quadruple \((\mu,\overline{\nu};\tilde{\mu},\tilde{\overline{\nu}})\). We call \(\mu\) and \(\tilde{\mu}\) the \(\ell_{1}(\omega\times 2)\)-part and \(\ell_{1}(\tilde{\omega}\times 2)\)-part of \(\lambda\) respectively.

Furthermore, from the discussion in Subsection 3.2, we can identify \(\mu\) and \(\tilde{\mu}\) with elements \(x\in\ell_{1}(\omega\times 2)\) and \(\tilde{x}\in\ell_{1}(\tilde{\omega}\times 2)\), and \(\overline{\nu}\) and \(\tilde{\overline{\nu}}\) with elements \(y\in\ell_{1}(\mathfrak{c}\times 2)\) and \(\tilde{y}\in\ell_{1}(\tilde{\mathfrak{c}}\times 2)\). In this way, the measure \(\lambda\) can be coded by the quadruple

\((x,y;\,\tilde{x},\tilde{y})\in\ell_{1}(\omega\times 2)\oplus\ell_{1}(\mathfrak{c}\times 2)\oplus\ell_{1}(\tilde{\omega}\times 2)\oplus\ell_{1}(\tilde{\mathfrak{c}}\times 2).\)
4.

Technical results

−

We recall some results of Plebanek and Salguero-Alarcón and make the natural adjustments to fit our framework.

4.1.

Separating sets of measures.

−

Since the nature of the underlying countable set is not important, in this section, we will discuss measures on \(\omega\) and \(\tilde{\omega}\). Throughout this section, we fix Boolean subalgebras \(\mathfrak{B}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\omega)\) and \(\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\omega})\) containing all finite subsets of \(\omega\) and \(\tilde{\omega}\), respectively. We state our results in general form, for arbitrary finitely-additive measures \(\lambda\) on \(\omega\cup\tilde{\omega}\), which we implicitly regard as the sum of a measure on \(\omega\) and a measure on \(\tilde{\omega}\). Accordingly, we adopt the slight abuse of notation \(M_{1}(\mathcal{P}(\omega),\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\omega}))\) for the collection of those measures with total variation at most one.

We shall employ the following analogue of separation, as given in .

Let \(M,M^{\prime}\subseteq M_{1}(\mathcal{P}(\omega),\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\omega}))\). We say that \((M,M^{\prime})\) is \((\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\)-separated with constant \(\varepsilon\) if there exist \(\varepsilon>0\), \(n,m\in\omega\) and \(B_{1},\dots,B_{n}\in\mathfrak{B}\), \(\tilde{B}_{1},\dots,\tilde{B}_{m}\in\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}\) such that

\(\max(\max_{i\leq n}|\lambda(B_{i})-\lambda^{\prime}(B_{i})|,\max_{j\leq m}|\lambda(\tilde{B}_{j})-\lambda^{\prime}(\tilde{B}_{j})|)\geq\varepsilon\)

for any \(\lambda\in M\) and \(\lambda^{\prime}\in M^{\prime}\). If the constant is not relevant, we simply say that \(M,M^{\prime}\) are \((\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\)-separated.

With this definition, we can get the following analogue of . The proof is identical and thus omitted.

Let \(M,M^{\prime}\subseteq M_{1}(\mathcal{P}(\omega),\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\omega}))\) and suppose there exist \(\varepsilon>0\) and simple \(\mathfrak{B}\)-measurable and \(\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}\)-measurable functions \(g:\omega\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(\tilde{g}:\tilde{\omega}\to\mathbb{R}\) such that

\(|\langle\lambda,g+\tilde{g}\rangle-\langle\lambda^{\prime},g+\tilde{g}\rangle|\geq\varepsilon,\)

for any \(\lambda\in M\) and \(\lambda^{\prime}\in M^{\prime}\). Then \((M,M^{\prime})\) is \((\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\)-separated.

Likewise, we have the following counterpart of . The proof is essentially the same, using now the compactness of \([-1,1]^{n}\times[-1,1]^{m}\). We omit the details.

Indeed, if \(\xi\) is a successor ordinal, say \(\xi=\eta+1\), then this is just (B3) for \(\eta\). Otherwise, if \(\xi\) is a limit ordinal, this follows from the fact that an increasing family of non-separating algebras is also not separating.

Therefore, we can apply Proposition 4.4 to the almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{Z}=\{Z(C):C\in\mathcal{C}\}\) and

  • –

    the family of algebra pairs \((\mathfrak{B}(\xi\setminus\{\alpha\}),\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}(\xi))\) and the lists

    \((\lambda^{\alpha}[J_{2}^{\alpha}],\lambda^{\alpha}[J_{1}^{\alpha}\setminus J_{2}^{\alpha}])\text{ and }(\lambda^{\alpha}[J_{1}^{\alpha}],\lambda^{\alpha}[J_{0}^{\alpha}\setminus J_{1}^{\alpha}])\)

    for \(\alpha<\xi\).

  • –

    The family of algebra pairs \((\mathfrak{B}(\xi),\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}(\xi\setminus\{\alpha\}))\) and the lists

    \((\gamma^{\alpha}[\tilde{J}_{2}^{\alpha}],\gamma^{\alpha}[\tilde{J}_{1}^{\alpha}\setminus\tilde{J}_{2}^{\alpha}])\text{ and }(\gamma^{\alpha}[\tilde{J}_{1}^{\alpha}],\gamma^{\alpha}[\tilde{J}_{0}^{\alpha}\setminus\tilde{J}_{1}^{\alpha}])\)

    for \(\alpha<\xi\).

Thus, we can find \(C\in\mathcal{C}\) such that:

  • –

    for every \(\alpha<\xi\), the pairs

    \((\lambda^{\alpha}[J_{2}^{\alpha}],\lambda^{\alpha}[J_{1}^{\alpha}\setminus J_{2}^{\alpha}])\hskip 5.0pt\text{ and }\hskip 5.0pt(\lambda^{\alpha}[J_{1}^{\alpha}],\lambda^{\alpha}[J_{0}^{\alpha}\setminus J_{1}^{\alpha}])\)

    are not separated even by the larger algebra pair \((\mathfrak{B}(\xi\setminus\{\alpha\})[Z(C)],\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}(\xi))\).

  • –

    For every \(\alpha<\xi\), the pairs

    \((\gamma^{\alpha}[\tilde{J}_{2}^{\alpha}],\gamma^{\alpha}[\tilde{J}_{1}^{\alpha}\setminus\tilde{J}_{2}^{\alpha}])\hskip 5.0pt\text{ and }\hskip 5.0pt(\gamma^{\alpha}[\tilde{J}_{1}^{\alpha}],\gamma^{\alpha}[\tilde{J}_{0}^{\alpha}\setminus\tilde{J}_{1}^{\alpha}])\)

    are not separated even by the larger algebra pair \((\mathfrak{B}(\xi)[Z(C)],\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}(\xi\setminus\{\alpha\}))\).

Having chosen \(C\in\mathcal{C}\), we repeat the procedure in the second copy. Since \((\tilde{\mu}_{\tilde{n}})_{\tilde{n}\in\tilde{\omega}}\), the \(\ell_{1}(\tilde{\omega}\times 2)\)-part of \((\gamma^{\xi}_{\tilde{n}})_{\tilde{n}\in\tilde{\omega}}\), is \(\sim\)-admissible, we can apply Lemma 4.7 continuum many times, each time for a cylinder \(\tilde{C}=\tilde{C}_{0}\times 2\in\tilde{\mathcal{C}}\), to obtain sets \(\tilde{J}_{2}(\tilde{C})\subseteq\tilde{J}_{1}(\tilde{C})\subseteq\tilde{J}_{0}(\tilde{C})\subseteq\tilde{C}_{0}\) and \(\tilde{Z}(\tilde{C})\subseteq\tilde{J}_{1}(\tilde{C})\times 2\), together with positive scalars \(\tilde{a}(\tilde{C})\) and \(\tilde{\delta}(\tilde{C})\) satisfying the conditions stated in the lemma. Again, by Lemma 4.3 and Remark 4.8 we may assume that the pairs

\((\gamma^{\xi}[\tilde{J}_{2}(\tilde{C})],\gamma^{\xi}[\tilde{J}_{1}(\tilde{C})\setminus\tilde{J}_{2}(\tilde{C})])\text{ and }(\gamma^{\xi}[\tilde{J}_{1}(\tilde{C}))],\gamma^{\xi}[\tilde{J}_{0}(\tilde{C})\setminus\tilde{J}_{1}(\tilde{C})])\)

are not \((\mathfrak{B}(\xi)[Z(C)],\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}(\xi))\)-separated.

We can invoke Proposition 4.4, this time for the almost disjoint family \(\tilde{\mathcal{Z}}=\{\tilde{Z}[\tilde{C}]:\tilde{C}\in\tilde{\mathcal{C}}\}\) and

  • –

    the family of algebra pairs \((\mathfrak{B}(\xi\setminus\{\alpha\})[Z(C)],\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}(\xi))\) and the lists

    \((\lambda^{\alpha}[J_{2}^{\alpha}],\lambda^{\alpha}[J_{1}^{\alpha}\setminus J_{2}^{\alpha}])\text{ and }(\lambda^{\alpha}[J_{1}^{\alpha}],\lambda^{\alpha}[J_{0}^{\alpha}\setminus J_{1}^{\alpha}])\)

    for \(\alpha<\xi\).

  • –

    The algebra pair \((\mathfrak{B}(\xi),\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}(\xi))\) and the pair

    \((\lambda^{\xi}[J_{2}(C)],\lambda^{\xi}[J_{1}(C)\setminus J_{2}(C)])\text{ and }(\lambda^{\xi}[J_{1}(C)],\lambda^{\xi}[J_{0}(C)\setminus J_{1}(C)]).\)
  • –

    The family of algebra pairs \((\mathfrak{B}(\xi)[Z(C)],\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}(\xi))\) and the lists

    \((\gamma^{\alpha}[\tilde{J}_{2}^{\alpha}],\gamma^{\alpha}[\tilde{J}_{1}^{\alpha}\setminus\tilde{J}_{2}^{\alpha}])\hskip 5.0pt\text{ and }\hskip 5.0pt(\gamma^{\alpha}[\tilde{J}_{1}^{\alpha}],\gamma^{\alpha}[\tilde{J}_{0}^{\alpha}\setminus\tilde{J}_{1}^{\alpha}])\)

    for \(\alpha<\xi\).

Hence, we can find \(\tilde{C}\in\tilde{\mathcal{C}}\) such that:

  • –

    for every \(\alpha<\xi\), the pairs

    \((\lambda^{\alpha}[J_{2}^{\alpha}],\lambda^{\alpha}[J_{1}^{\alpha}\setminus J_{2}^{\alpha}])\hskip 5.0pt\text{ and }\hskip 5.0pt(\lambda^{\alpha}[J_{1}^{\alpha}],\lambda^{\alpha}[J_{0}^{\alpha}\setminus J_{1}^{\alpha}])\)

    are not separated even by the larger algebra pair \((\mathfrak{B}(\xi\setminus\{\alpha\})[Z(C)],\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}(\xi)[\tilde{Z}(\tilde{C})])\).

  • –

    The pairs

    \((\lambda^{\xi}[J_{2}(C)],\lambda^{\xi}[J_{1}(C)\setminus J_{2}(C)])\text{ and }(\lambda^{\xi}[J_{1}(C)],\lambda^{\xi}[J_{0}(C)\setminus J_{1}(C)]).\)

    are not separated even by the larger algebra pair \((\mathfrak{B}(\xi),\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}(\xi)[\tilde{Z}(\tilde{C})])\).

  • –

    For every \(\alpha<\xi\), the pairs

    \((\gamma^{\alpha}[\tilde{J}_{2}^{\alpha}],\gamma^{\alpha}[\tilde{J}_{1}^{\alpha}\setminus\tilde{J}_{2}^{\alpha}])\hskip 5.0pt\text{ and }\hskip 5.0pt(\gamma^{\alpha}[\tilde{J}_{1}^{\alpha}],\gamma^{\alpha}[\tilde{J}_{0}^{\alpha}\setminus\tilde{J}_{1}^{\alpha}])\)

    are not separated even by the larger algebra pair \((\mathfrak{B}(\xi)[Z(C)],\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}(\xi\setminus\{\alpha\})[\tilde{Z}(\tilde{C})])\).

Finally, set

  1. (i’)

    \(J_{2}^{\xi}=J_{2}(C)\), \(J_{1}^{\xi}=J_{1}(C)\), \(J_{0}^{\xi}=J_{0}(C)\),

  2. (ii’)

    \(\tilde{J}_{2}^{\xi}=\tilde{J}_{2}(\tilde{C})\), \(\tilde{J}_{1}^{\xi}=\tilde{J}_{1}(\tilde{C})\), \(\tilde{J}_{0}^{\xi}=\tilde{J}_{0}(\tilde{C})\),

  3. (iii’)

    \(A_{\xi}=J_{1}(C)\times 2\), \(B_{\xi}^{0}=Z(C)\), \(B_{\xi}^{1}=A_{\xi}\setminus B_{\xi}^{0}\); \(\tilde{A}_{\xi}=\tilde{J}_{1}(\tilde{C})\times 2\), \(\tilde{B}_{\xi}^{0}=\tilde{Z}(\tilde{C})\), \(\tilde{B}_{\xi}^{1}=\tilde{A}_{\xi}\setminus\tilde{B}_{\xi}^{0}\),

  4. (iv’)

    \(a_{\xi}=a(C)\), \(\tilde{a}_{\xi}=\tilde{a}(\tilde{C})\), \(\delta_{\xi}=\delta(C)\) and \(\tilde{\delta}_{\xi}=\tilde{\delta}(\tilde{C})\).

By construction, conditions (B1)–(B3) are satisfied. Indeed, (B1)–(B2) are precisely (A1) in Lemma 4.7, which hold by our choices in the construction. Moreover, (B3) follows directly from the construction, since we ensured an appropriate choice guaranteeing separation of measures. This completes the induction.

With the construction completed according to the inductive procedure, we now define the almost disjoint families

\(\mathcal{A}=\{A_{\xi}:\xi<\mathfrak{c}\},\hskip 3.0pt\tilde{\mathcal{A}}=\{\tilde{A}_{\xi}:\xi<\mathfrak{c}\},\hskip 3.0pt\mathcal{B}=\{B_{\xi}^{0},B_{\xi}^{1}:\xi<\mathfrak{c}\},\text{ and }\tilde{\mathcal{B}}=\{\tilde{B}_{\xi}^{0},\tilde{B}_{\xi}^{1}:\xi<\mathfrak{c}\}.\)

These families will ensure that the corresponding \(X\) and \(\tilde{X}\) are not isomorphic to Banach lattices, as we will demonstrate in the next section.

6.

Proof of Theorem 1.1

−
Correction to the error estimate

In equation (8) and the following estimate, 4r + 3 is replaced by 4 + 3r. This part of the argument assumes r ≥ 0; the general bound is 4 + 3|r|.

Let \(\mathcal{A},\tilde{\mathcal{A}},\mathcal{B}\) and \(\tilde{\mathcal{B}}\) be the almost disjoint families built in Section 5. We show that, for these families, the spaces \(X\) and \(\tilde{X}\) such that

\(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B},\tilde{\mathcal{B}})=X\oplus\tilde{X,}\)

defined as in Subsection 3.4, are not isomorphic to Banach lattices. Since the proofs for \(X\) and \(\tilde{X}\) are identical, we only do it for the former.

Observe that \(X\) is a \(1\)-complemented subspace of \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B},\tilde{\mathcal{B}})\). Therefore \(X^{*}\) is \(1\)-complemented in \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B},\tilde{\mathcal{B}})^{*}\equiv\ell_{1}(K_{\mathcal{B}}\cup K_{\tilde{\mathcal{B}}})\) and hence it is linearly isometric to \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\) for some \(\Gamma\). Furthermore, observe that

\(\{\delta_{(n,0}),\delta_{(n,1)}:n\in\omega\}\cup\{\delta_{(\tilde{n},0}),\delta_{(\tilde{n},1)}:\tilde{n}\in\tilde{\omega}\}\)

is a \(1\)-norming set for \(\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B},\tilde{\mathcal{B}})\) and thus, in particular, \(X\) has a countable \(1\)-norming set. That is, the conditions of Proposition 3.4 are satisfied.

For convenience, we also state the following consequences of the construction. Recall that \(\{(\lambda_{n}^{\xi})_{n\in\omega}:\xi<\mathfrak{c}\}\) is an ordering of \(\Phi\), as described in the construction, and that we have a decomposition \(\lambda_{n}^{\xi}=(\mu_{n}^{\xi}+\overline{\nu}_{n}^{\xi})+\tilde{\nu}_{n}^{\xi}\).

  1. (P1)

    For every \(\xi<\mathfrak{c}\) let \(b_{\xi}=\inf_{n\in\omega}|\mu_{n}^{\xi}(\{(n,0)\})|>0\). By (B1), there exist \(a_{\xi}\geq b_{\xi}\) and \(0<\delta_{\xi}<b_{\xi}/11\) such that

    \(\mu^{\xi}_{n}(B_{\xi}^{0})-\mu^{\xi}_{n}(B_{\xi}^{1})\approx_{3\delta_{\xi}}\begin{cases}2a_{\xi}&\text{if }n\in J^{\xi}_{2},\\ -2a_{\xi}&\text{if }n\in J^{\xi}_{1}\setminus J^{\xi}_{2},\\ 0&\text{if }n\in J^{\xi}_{0}\setminus J^{\xi}_{1}.\end{cases}\)
  2. (P2)

    For any \(\xi<\mathfrak{c}\), the pairs

    \((\lambda^{\xi}[J_{2}^{\xi}],\lambda^{\xi}[J_{1}^{\xi}\setminus J_{2}^{\xi}])\text{ and }(\lambda^{\xi}[J_{1}^{\xi}],\lambda^{\xi}[J_{0}^{\xi}\setminus J_{1}^{\xi}])\)

    are not \((\mathfrak{B}(\mathfrak{c}\setminus\{\xi\}),\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\)-separated. This follows since (B3) holds for every \(\eta<\mathfrak{c}\), and the union of an increasing family of non-separating algebras is again not separating.

We are now ready for the proof.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.Fold proof

By Proposition 3.4 and the previous discussion, it is enough to show that \(X\) has the (DP). Thus, we start by fixing a norming sequence \((e^{*}_{n})_{n\in\omega}\) for \(X\). Our objective is to find \(f\in X\) such that no \(g\in X\) satisfies

\(\langle e^{*}_{n},g\rangle=|\langle e_{n}^{*},f\rangle|\hskip 5.0pt\text{ for every }n\in\omega.\)

Since \((e_{n}^{*})_{n\in\omega}\) is norming for \(X\) and \(f_{k}=\mathds{1}_{(k,0)}-\mathds{1}_{(k,1)}\in Y\subseteq X\) (see Subsection 3.4 for the definition of \(Y\)), passing to a subsequence of \((e_{n}^{*})_{n\in\omega}\), we may assume that

\(0<\inf_{n\in\omega}|\langle e_{n}^{*},f_{n}\rangle|.\)

From Remarks 3.5 and 3.6, we can write \(e_{n}^{*}=(\mu_{n}+\overline{\nu}_{n})+\tilde{\nu}_{n}\), so that \(\mu_{n}(\{(k,0)\})+\mu_{n}(\{(k,1)\})=0\) for every \(k\in\omega\), \(\overline{\nu}_{n}(B_{\alpha}^{0})+\overline{\nu}_{n}(B_{\alpha}^{1})=0\) for every \(\alpha<\mathfrak{c}\) and \(\left\lVert e^{*}_{n}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert\mu_{n}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert\overline{\nu}_{n}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert\tilde{\nu}_{n}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 1\). In other words, the coding of \(e_{n}^{*}\) is of Type-1.

Observe that

\(0<\frac{1}{2}\inf_{n\in\omega}|\langle e_{n}^{*},f_{n}\rangle|=\inf_{n\in\omega}|e_{n}^{*}(\{(n,0)\})|=\inf_{n\in\omega}|\mu_{n}(\{(n,0)\})|=:b.\)

From the above discussion and the construction in Section 5, we can find \(\xi<\mathfrak{c}\) such that \((e_{n}^{*})_{n\in\omega}=(\lambda^{\xi}_{n})_{n\in\omega}\). For convenience, we drop the \(\xi\) from the measures, and simply write \((e_{n}^{*})_{n\in\omega}=(\lambda_{n})_{n\in\omega}=(\mu_{n}+\overline{\nu}_{n}+\tilde{\nu}_{n})_{n\in\omega}\). Similarly, we also denote \(\delta\equiv\delta_{\xi}\) and \(a\equiv a_{\xi}\) according to (P1).

Recall that, from the way the enumeration was carried out, for any \(n\in\omega\) and \(i=0,1\) we have \(\overline{\nu}_{n}(B_{\alpha}^{i})=0\) whenever \(\alpha\geq\xi\). We claim that

\(f=\mathds{1}_{B^{0}_{\xi}}-\mathds{1}_{B^{1}_{\xi}}\in Y\subseteq X\)

witnesses (DP), which will finish the proof. Assume the contrary, so that we can find \(g\in X\) such that

\(\langle\lambda_{n},g\rangle=|\langle\lambda_{n},f\rangle|\hskip 5.0pt\text{ for every }n\in\omega.\)

Note that \(\langle\overline{\nu}_{n},f\rangle=0\) since \(\overline{\nu}_{n}(B_{\xi}^{i})=0\) for every \(n\in\omega\) and \(i=0,1\). Clearly, \(\langle\tilde{\nu}_{n},f\rangle=0\) and thus \(\langle\lambda_{n},f\rangle=\langle\mu_{n},f\rangle\).

Since the subspace

\(\{h+\tilde{h}:h\in Y\text{ simple }\mathfrak{B}\text{-measurable, and }\tilde{h}\in\operatorname{JL}(\tilde{A})\text{ simple }\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}\text{-measurable}\}\)

is dense in \(X\), it follows that we can find a simple \(\mathfrak{B}\)-measurable \(h\in Y\) and a simple \(\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}\)-measurable function \(\tilde{h}\in\operatorname{JL}(\tilde{\mathcal{A}})\) such that \(\left\lVert g-(h+\tilde{h})\right\rVert<\delta\). Hence

\(|\langle\mu_{n},f\rangle|=|\langle\lambda_{n},f\rangle|=\langle\lambda_{n},g\rangle\approx_{\delta}\langle\lambda_{n},h+\tilde{h}\rangle,\hskip 5.0pt\text{ for every }n\in\omega.\)

Without loss of generality, we may assume that \(h=rf+s\) where \(r\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(s\in Y\) is a simple \(\mathfrak{B}(\mathfrak{c\setminus\{\xi\}})\)-measurable function, so that

\(|\langle\mu_{n},f\rangle|\approx_{\delta}r\langle\mu_{n},f\rangle+\langle\lambda_{n},s+\tilde{h}\rangle,\hskip 5.0pt\text{ for every }n\in\omega.\) (4)

Furthermore, we may assume that \(r\geq 0\), the case \(r<0\) follows in the same way. Observe that (P1) gives

\(\langle\mu_{n},f\rangle=\mu_{n}(B_{\xi}^{0})-\mu_{n}(B_{\xi}^{1})\approx_{3\delta}\begin{cases}2a&\text{if }n\in J_{2}^{\xi},\\ -2a&\text{if }n\in J^{\xi}_{1}\setminus J_{2}^{\xi},\\ 0&\text{if }n\in J_{0}^{\xi}\setminus J^{\xi}_{1},\end{cases}\) (5)

and thus in particular

\(|\langle\mu_{n},f\rangle|\approx_{3\delta}\begin{cases}2a&\text{if }n\in J_{1}^{\xi},\\ 0&\text{if }n\in J_{0}^{\xi}\setminus J^{\xi}_{1}.\end{cases}\) (6)

Combining (4), (5) and (6) yields

\(\begin{cases}2a\approx_{\delta(4+3r)}2ra+\langle\lambda_{n},s+\tilde{h}\rangle&\text{if }n\in J_{2}^{\xi},\\ 2a\approx_{\delta(4+3r)}-2ra+\langle\lambda_{n},s+\tilde{h}\rangle&\text{if }n\in J^{\xi}_{1}\setminus J_{2}^{\xi},\\ 0\approx_{\delta(4+3r)}\langle\lambda_{n},s+\tilde{h}\rangle&\text{if }n\in J_{0}^{\xi}\setminus J^{\xi}_{1}.\end{cases}\) (7)

Suppose first that \(0\leq r\leq 1/2\), the first two equations in (7) give

\(\langle\lambda_{n},s+\tilde{h}\rangle\geq 2(1-r)a-\delta(4+3r)\geq a-\frac{11}{2}\delta,\hskip 5.0pt\text{ for every }n\in J_{1}^{\xi},\)

while the third equation in (7) yields

\(\langle\lambda_{n},s+\tilde{h}\rangle\leq\delta(4+3r)\leq\frac{11}{2}\delta,\hskip 5.0pt\text{ for every }n\in J_{0}^{\xi}\setminus J^{\xi}_{1}.\)

Therefore, since \(a\geq b>11\delta\), we get

\(\langle\lambda_{n},s+\tilde{h}\rangle-\langle\lambda_{k},s+\tilde{h}\rangle\geq a-11\delta>0\)

for any \(n\in J_{1}^{\xi}\) and \(k\in J_{0}^{\xi}\setminus J_{1}^{\xi}\). Lemma 4.2 now gives that the pair

\(\{\lambda_{n}:n\in J_{1}^{\xi}\}=\lambda_{n}[J_{1}^{\xi}]\hskip 5.0pt\text{ and }\hskip 5.0pt\{\lambda_{n}:n\in J_{0}^{\xi}\setminus J_{1}^{\xi}\}=\lambda_{n}[J_{0}^{\xi}\setminus J_{1}^{\xi}]\)

is \((\mathfrak{B}(\mathfrak{c}\setminus\{\xi\}),\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\)-separated, which contradicts (P2).

Suppose now that \(r>1/2\), then by (7) we deduce that

\(\displaystyle\langle\lambda_{n},s+\tilde{h}\rangle-\langle\lambda_{k},s+\tilde{h}\rangle\) \(\displaystyle\geq 2a(1+r)-\delta(4+3r)-\bigl(2a(1-r)+\delta(4+3r)\bigr)\)
\(\displaystyle=2r(2a-3\delta)-8\delta\geq 2a-11\delta>0.\)

for any \(n\in J_{1}^{\xi}\setminus J_{2}^{\xi}\) and \(k\in J_{2}^{\xi}\). By Lemma 4.2 we have that the pair

\(\{\lambda_{n}:n\in J_{2}^{\xi}\}=\lambda_{n}[J_{2}^{\xi}]\hskip 5.0pt\text{ and }\hskip 5.0pt\{\lambda_{n}:n\in J_{1}^{\xi}\setminus J^{\xi}_{2}\}=\lambda_{n}[J_{1}^{\xi}\setminus J^{\xi}_{2}]\)

is \((\mathfrak{B}(\mathfrak{c}\setminus\{\xi\}),\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\)-separated, which again contradicts (P2). This finishes the proof. ∎

results.statementHtml:
There exist a compact Hausdorff space \(L\) and Banach spaces \(X\) and \(\tilde{X}\) such that

\(C(L)\simeq X\oplus\tilde{X},\)

and neither \(X\) nor \(\tilde{X}\) is isomorphic to a Banach lattice.
Note that this provides a key insight: the \(\ell_{1}(\omega)\)-part has, in a sense, a universal character, as it extends uniquely as a measure to any Boolean subalgebra of \(\mathcal{P}(\omega)\).

Let \(X\) be a Banach space and \(0<c\leq 1\). We say that a sequence \((e_{n}^{*})_{n\in\omega}\subseteq B_{X^{*}}\) is \(c\)-norming if

\(c\left\lVert x\right\rVert\leq\sup_{n\in\omega}|\langle e^{*}_{n},x\rangle|\)

for every \(x\in X\). If the constant \(c\) is not relevant, we simply say that the sequence \((e_{n}^{*})_{n\in\omega}\subseteq B_{X^{*}}\) is norming.

Corrected norming inequality

The arXiv text reverses this bound. The lower bound displayed here is the convention used in the argument and in Lean; see More detail for the reason.

We say that a Banach space \(X\) has the Desired Property of De Hevia, Martínez-Cervantes, Salguero-Alarcón, and Tradacete, abbreviated (DP), if for every norming sequence \((e_{n}^{*})_{n\in\omega}\) in \(B_{X^{*}}\) there exists an element \(f\in X\) such that no element \(g\in X\) satisfies

\(\langle e_{n}^{*},g\rangle=|\langle e_{n}^{*},f\rangle|\quad\text{for every }n\in\omega.\) (DP)

Let \(X\) be a Banach space with a countable norming set. Suppose that \(X^{*}\) is isomorphic to \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\) for some index set \(\Gamma\). Then, the following statements are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    \(X\) is isomorphic to a Banach lattice.

  2. (b)

    \(X\) is isomorphic to a sublattice of \(\ell_{\infty}\).

  3. (c)

    \(X\) does not have the (DP). That is, there exists a norming sequence \((e_{n}^{*})_{n\in\omega}\) in \(B_{X^{*}}\) such that for every \(f\in X\) there is an element \(g\in X\) such that

    \(\langle e_{n}^{*},g\rangle=|\langle e_{n}^{*},f\rangle|,\quad\text{for every }n\in\omega.\)

Let \(x^{*}\in X^{*}\). Then \(x^{*}Q\in\operatorname{JL}(\mathcal{B},\tilde{\mathcal{B}})^{*}=M(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\), so that every functional on \(X\) can be seen as an element on \(M(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\) vanishing on all cylinders from \(\mathfrak{B}\). In other words, we have an embedding

\(X^{*}\to M(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}),\quad x^{*}\mapsto x^{*}Q.\)

Analogous considerations apply to \(\tilde{x}^{*}\in\tilde{X}^{*}\).

We will reserve the symbols \(\lambda\) and \(\gamma\) for elements in \(M_{1}(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\). Observe that we have a decomposition \(\lambda=\nu+\tilde{\nu}\) where \(\nu\in M_{1}(\mathfrak{B})\) and \(\tilde{\nu}\in M_{1}(\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\) (with their natural interpretations). From the discussion in Subsection 3.2, we can further express \(\nu=\mu+\overline{\nu}\) where \(\mu\in\ell_{1}(\omega\times 2)\), \(\overline{\nu}\) vanishes on finite sets and \(|\overline{\nu}|(B)\not=0\) for at most countably many \(B\in\mathcal{B}\). Identical considerations apply for \(\tilde{\nu}\). Using these decompositions we can write \(\lambda=\nu+\tilde{\nu}=(\mu+\overline{\nu})+(\tilde{\mu}+\tilde{\overline{\nu}})\). Therefore, a measure \(\lambda\in M_{1}(\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\) can be seem as a quadruple \((\mu,\overline{\nu};\tilde{\mu},\tilde{\overline{\nu}})\). We call \(\mu\) and \(\tilde{\mu}\) the \(\ell_{1}(\omega\times 2)\)-part and \(\ell_{1}(\tilde{\omega}\times 2)\)-part of \(\lambda\) respectively.

Furthermore, from the discussion in Subsection 3.2, we can identify \(\mu\) and \(\tilde{\mu}\) with elements \(x\in\ell_{1}(\omega\times 2)\) and \(\tilde{x}\in\ell_{1}(\tilde{\omega}\times 2)\), and \(\overline{\nu}\) and \(\tilde{\overline{\nu}}\) with elements \(y\in\ell_{1}(\mathfrak{c}\times 2)\) and \(\tilde{y}\in\ell_{1}(\tilde{\mathfrak{c}}\times 2)\). In this way, the measure \(\lambda\) can be coded by the quadruple

\((x,y;\,\tilde{x},\tilde{y})\in\ell_{1}(\omega\times 2)\oplus\ell_{1}(\mathfrak{c}\times 2)\oplus\ell_{1}(\tilde{\omega}\times 2)\oplus\ell_{1}(\tilde{\mathfrak{c}}\times 2).\)

Let \(M,M^{\prime}\subseteq M_{1}(\mathcal{P}(\omega),\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\omega}))\). We say that \((M,M^{\prime})\) is \((\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\)-separated with constant \(\varepsilon\) if there exist \(\varepsilon>0\), \(n,m\in\omega\) and \(B_{1},\dots,B_{n}\in\mathfrak{B}\), \(\tilde{B}_{1},\dots,\tilde{B}_{m}\in\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}\) such that

\(\max(\max_{i\leq n}|\lambda(B_{i})-\lambda^{\prime}(B_{i})|,\max_{j\leq m}|\lambda(\tilde{B}_{j})-\lambda^{\prime}(\tilde{B}_{j})|)\geq\varepsilon\)

for any \(\lambda\in M\) and \(\lambda^{\prime}\in M^{\prime}\). If the constant is not relevant, we simply say that \(M,M^{\prime}\) are \((\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\)-separated.

Let \(M,M^{\prime}\subseteq M_{1}(\mathcal{P}(\omega),\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\omega}))\) and suppose there exist \(\varepsilon>0\) and simple \(\mathfrak{B}\)-measurable and \(\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}\)-measurable functions \(g:\omega\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(\tilde{g}:\tilde{\omega}\to\mathbb{R}\) such that

\(|\langle\lambda,g+\tilde{g}\rangle-\langle\lambda^{\prime},g+\tilde{g}\rangle|\geq\varepsilon,\)

for any \(\lambda\in M\) and \(\lambda^{\prime}\in M^{\prime}\). Then \((M,M^{\prime})\) is \((\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\)-separated.

Suppose that \(|\mathfrak{B}|<\mathfrak{c}\) and \(|\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}|<\mathfrak{c}\). Then, for every infinite subset \(M\subseteq M_{1}(\mathcal{P}(\omega),\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\omega}))\) the pair \((M^{\prime},M\setminus M^{\prime})\) can be \((\mathfrak{B},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\)-separated for fewer than \(\mathfrak{c}\) many sets \(M^{\prime}\subseteq M\).

Suppose \(I\) is an index set with \(|I|<\mathfrak{c}\) and that we are given:

  1. (i)

    a list \(\{(\mathfrak{B}_{j},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}_{j}):j\in I\}\) of pairs of Boolean subalgebras of \(\mathcal{P}(\omega)\) and \(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\omega})\) respectively, such that, for every \(j\in I\), \(\operatorname{fin}(\omega)\subseteq\mathfrak{B}_{j}\), \(\operatorname{fin}(\tilde{\omega})\subseteq\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}_{j}\) and \(|\mathfrak{B}_{j}|\leq|I|\), \(|\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}_{j}|\leq|I|\).

  2. (ii)

    a list \(\{(M_{j},M^{\prime}_{j}):j\in I\}\) of pairs of subsets of \(M_{1}(\mathcal{P}(\omega),\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\omega}))\) such that, for every \(j\in J\), the pair \((M_{j},M^{\prime}_{j})\) is not \((\mathfrak{B}_{j},\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}_{j})\)-separated.

Then for every almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\mathcal{P(\omega)}\) with \(|\mathcal{Z}|=\mathfrak{c}\) there exists \(Z\in\mathcal{Z}\) such that for every \(j\in J\), the pair \((M_{j},M^{\prime}_{j})\) is not \((\mathfrak{B}_{j}[Z],\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}_{j})\)-separated. An analogous result holds for any almost disjoint family \(\tilde{\mathcal{Z}}\subseteq\mathcal{P(\tilde{\omega})}\) with \(|\tilde{\mathcal{Z}}|=\mathfrak{c}\).

Suppose that for a given \(M,M^{\prime}\subseteq M_{1}(\mathcal{P}(\omega),\mathcal{P}(\tilde{\omega}))\), there are:

  1. (a)

    \(n\in\omega\), \(m\in\omega\), \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(k>\frac{12n}{\varepsilon}\)

  2. (b)

    almost disjoint sets \(Z_{1},\dots,Z_{k}\subseteq\omega\),

  3. (c)

    \(A_{1},B_{1},\dots,A_{n},B_{n}\in\mathfrak{B}\) and \(\tilde{A}_{1},\dots,\tilde{A}_{m}\in\tilde{\mathfrak{B}}\)

such that, for every \(1\leq j\leq k\), the pair \((M,M^{\prime})\) is \((\mathfrak{B}[Z_{j}],\tilde{\mathfrak{B}})\)-separated, with constant \(\varepsilon\), by the sets

\(Y_{j,i}=(A_{i}\cap Z_{j})\cup(B_{i}\cap Z_{j}^{c}),\hskip 5.0pt1\leq i\leq n\hskip 10.0pt\text{ and }\tilde{A}_{l},\hskip 10.0pt1\leq l\leq m.\)

We say that a sequence \((\mu_{n})_{n\in\omega}\) in the unit ball of \(\ell_{1}(\omega\times 2)\) is admissible if

  1. (a)

    \(\mu_{n}(\{(k,0)\})=-\mu_{n}(\{(k,1)\})\) for all \(n\in\omega\) and \(k\in\omega\),

  2. (b)

    \(\inf_{n\in\omega}|\mu_{n}(\{(n,0)\})|>0\).

Similarly, a sequence \((\tilde{\mu}_{\tilde{n}})_{\tilde{n}\in\tilde{\omega}}\) in the unit ball of \(\ell_{1}(\tilde{\omega}\times 2)\) is \(\sim\)-admissible if

  1. (a)

    \(\tilde{\mu}_{\tilde{n}}(\{(\tilde{k},0)\})=-\tilde{\mu}_{\tilde{n}}(\{(\tilde{k},1)\})\) for all \(\tilde{n}\in\tilde{\omega}\) and \(\tilde{k}\in\tilde{\omega}\),

  2. (b)

    \(\inf_{\tilde{n}\in\tilde{\omega}}|\tilde{\mu}_{\tilde{n}}(\{(\tilde{n},0)\})|>0\).

Let \(C=C_{0}\times 2\subseteq\omega\times 2\) be a cylinder, \((\mu_{n})_{n\in\omega}\) be an admissible sequence and \(b=\inf_{n\in\omega}|\mu_{n}(\{(n,0)\})|\). Then there exist:

  • –

    three infinite sets \(J_{2}\subseteq J_{1}\subseteq J_{0}\subseteq C_{0}\) with \(J_{0}\setminus J_{1}\), \(J_{1}\setminus J_{2}\) infinite,

  • –

    a set \(Z\) splitting the cylinder \(J_{1}\times 2\),

  • –

    two positive constants \(a\geq b\) and \(0<\delta<b/11\),

such that the following holds:

\(\mu_{n}(Z)-\mu_{n}((J_{1}\times 2)\setminus Z)\approx_{3\delta}\begin{cases}2a&\text{if }n\in J_{2},\\ -2a&\text{if }n\in J_{1}\setminus J_{2},\\ 0&\text{if }n\in J_{0}\setminus J_{1}.\end{cases}\) (A1)

Similar considerations apply for a cylinder \(\tilde{C}=\tilde{C}_{0}\times 2\subseteq\tilde{\omega}\times 2\) and a \(\sim\)-admissible sequence \((\tilde{\mu}_{\tilde{n}})_{\tilde{n}\in\tilde{\omega}}\).

In Lemma 4.7, the sets \(J_{1}\) and \(J_{2}\) may be replaced by any infinite subsets of themselves; in particular, there are continuum many ways to choose them. Observe that, if we do this replacement, then (A1) is still satisfied with the same values of \(\delta\) and \(a\).

readingRevisions.html: We prove the strengthened selection by Haydon’s counting argument. The following form of the finite separation estimate allows arbitrary subsets inside each member of an almost disjoint family.

Let \(M,M'\subseteq M_1(\mathcal P(\omega),\mathcal P(\widetilde\omega))\), and let \(n,m,k\in\mathbb N\) and \(\varepsilon>0\). Suppose that \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\subseteq\omega\) have pairwise finite intersections and \(k>12n/\varepsilon\).

Let \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\in\mathfrak B\), \(E_{j,i}\subseteq C_j\) for \(1\leq j\leq k\), \(1\leq i\leq n\), and \(\widetilde A_1,\ldots,\widetilde A_m\in\widetilde{\mathfrak B}\). Suppose that, for every \(j\), the pair \((M,M')\) is separated with constant \(\varepsilon\) by

\[Y_{j,i}=E_{j,i}\cup(D_i\setminus C_j)\quad(1\leq i\leq n),\qquad \widetilde A_s\quad(1\leq s\leq m).\]

Then \(M\) and \(M'\) are separated by \((\mathfrak B,\widetilde{\mathfrak B})\).

footnote.title: Strengthened lemma, as in thesis Lemma 6.6
footnote.html: The published lemma uses fixed sets \(A_i\in\mathfrak B\) and \(E_{j,i}=A_i\cap C_j\). For the strengthened selection, the subsets \(E_{j,i}\subseteq C_j\) must be allowed to vary with \(j\). The finite-variation proof below establishes this stronger version.

readingRevisions.html:
Suppose that \(M\) and \(M'\) are not separated by the original algebra pair. Set

\[F=\bigcup_{1\leq j<l\leq k}(C_j\cap C_l).\]

Then \(F\) is finite and the sets \(C_j\setminus F\) are pairwise disjoint. The sets \(D_i\), \(E_{j,i}\cap F\) and \(D_i\cap C_j\cap F\) belong to \(\mathfrak B\). By nonseparation, choose \(\lambda\in M\) and \(\lambda'\in M'\) so that \(\rho=\lambda-\lambda'\) has absolute value less than \(\varepsilon/6\) on all these sets and on \(\widetilde A_1,\ldots,\widetilde A_m\). Put

\[v_{j,i}=|\rho(E_{j,i}\setminus F)|+|\rho((D_i\cap C_j)\setminus F)|.\]

Since \(\rho(Y_{j,i})=\rho(D_i)+\rho(E_{j,i})-\rho(D_i\cap C_j)\),

\[|\rho(Y_{j,i})|<\varepsilon/2+v_{j,i}.\]

The separating tests from the second copy all have absolute value less than \(\varepsilon/6\). Hence, for each \(j\), some \(i\) satisfies \(|\rho(Y_{j,i})|\geq\varepsilon\), and consequently \(\sum_{i=1}^n v_{j,i}>\varepsilon/2\). Pairwise disjointness of the sets \(C_j\setminus F\), together with \(\|\rho\|\leq2\), gives \(\sum_{j=1}^k v_{j,i}\leq4\) for each \(i\). Thus

\[k\varepsilon/2<\sum_{j=1}^k\sum_{i=1}^n v_{j,i}\leq4n,\]

contrary to \(k>12n/\varepsilon\).

□

Proof of Proposition 4.4Fold proof

The conclusion is immediate if \(I\) is empty. Otherwise suppose that it fails for every \(C\in\mathcal C\). For each such \(C\), choose \(Z_C\subseteq C\) and \(i\in I\) for which separation occurs. Every member of \(\mathfrak B_i[Z_C,C\setminus Z_C]\) agrees outside \(C\) with a member of \(\mathfrak B_i\), and therefore has the form

\[E\cup(D\setminus C),\qquad E\subseteq C,\quad D\in\mathfrak B_i.\]

There are at most \(|I|+\aleph_0\) choices of \(i\), the numbers \(n,m\) of separating sets, a positive rational separation constant \(\varepsilon\), and the finite lists \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\in\mathfrak B_i\) and \(\widetilde A_1,\ldots,\widetilde A_m\in\widetilde{\mathfrak B}_i\). Since \(|\mathcal C|=\mathfrak c\), one choice occurs for infinitely many members of \(\mathcal C\). Choose \(k>12n/\varepsilon\) of them.

The sets \(E_{j,l}\subseteq C_j\) may vary with \(j\), but Lemma 4.5 applies. It follows that \(M_i\) and \(M_i'\) were already separated by the original algebra pair, a contradiction. Interchanging the two copies gives the other case.

□

remark-3-1.note: The atomic part of a functional is treated in the formal charge representation. The full JL dual also has a coordinate at infinity, which the Lean construction keeps explicitly; the paper’s printed coordinates alone do not determine every functional.

definition-3-2.note: The intended lower norming bound is c‖x‖ ≤ supₙ |eₙ*(x)|. The reversed inequality in the arXiv text is corrected in this reading edition.

definition-3-3.note: DP quantifies over every norming sequence: for each sequence, some vector has no vector realizing all its coordinatewise absolute values. The corrected norming convention is used.

proposition-3-4.note: All three conditions are proved equivalent under the countable norming and ℓ¹-dual hypotheses. The ordered dual representation is proved within the formalisation; it is not an additional assumption.

remark-3-5.note: The formalisation constructs norm-preserving extensions of functionals from the crossed summands and proves their charge representation. This remark is explanatory, with no separate theorem certificate.

remark-3-6.note: The formal paired representation retains the two coordinates at infinity in addition to the isolated and family coordinates. The antisymmetric condition removes only the appropriate infinity coordinate.

definition-4-1.note: Separation is expressed using a finite family of tests from the two Boolean algebras and a uniform positive gap.

lemma-4-2.note: The simple functions are represented as finite linear combinations of characteristic functions. This analytic separation lemma is combined with the formal charge representation to obtain the paper’s measure formulation.

lemma-4-3.note: The cardinality estimate is proved for the actual pair of measure algebras. The argument does not assume the continuum hypothesis.

proposition-4-4.note: The reading edition gives the strengthened selection of thesis Proposition 6.7. Lean proves that one supporting set works for every split, preserving nonseparation after both halves are adjoined. The journal article states only the one-set version; its formal proof remains available among the proof choices.

lemma-4-5.note: The strengthened statement is thesis Lemma 6.6: the sets inside each supporting set may vary freely. Lean proves this local finite-variation estimate, using the stronger numerical bound with constant 8 while retaining the stated hypothesis with 12.

definition-4-6.note: The sequence lies in the ℓ¹ unit ball, is antisymmetric on each fibre, and has a uniformly positive diagonal coefficient.

lemma-4-7.note: The selection theorem constructs the nested infinite sets and the splitting, with the strict three-level estimates. No selection principle is added as a hypothesis.

remark-4-8.note: The formal construction uses restrictions of the selected infinite sets and the corresponding estimates. This observation has no separate numbered declaration in the companion.
